solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Greyish-brown VW Golf stops being in motion (4,6)

indicators.note: G stops, or plugs, the gap between the other two pieces

blocks.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown, as in a dun horse
G is Golf in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A dull-coloured Volkswagen Golf finally pulls up and parks.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'VW Golf' one car; in fact VW is the Beetle and Golf is only the letter G, lodged inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A dung beetle is a creature forever on the move, rolling its ball of dung along.

entries.clue: Patsy expected to absorb pressure (4)

indicators.note: to absorb is to soak something up and hold it inside, so DUE takes P into its middle

blocks.note: due = expected, as a train is due
P is the symbol for pressure

annotation.surface: Someone set up as the fall guy is expected to take the strain.
annotation.walkthrough: P goes inside DUE after the U.
annotation.definitionFit: A patsy and a dupe are both people easily fooled or made to take the blame.

entries.clue: North and east German area left Joe with a sense of wistfulness (9)

blocks.note: a GI Joe is an American soldier
the final 'a' is used as it stands

annotation.surface: Someone who left a region of north-east Germany now feels homesick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'East German' reads as a nationality, but it asks for the German word for east. Only 'with' links; the 'a' after it is the last letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Nostalgia is a wistful longing for the past.

entries.clue: Landmark new Waterloo block with parking thrown in (9,5)

indicators.note: a new version of the letters is a rearranged one
something thrown in is included as an extra, so P joins the letters being rearranged

blocks.note: P = parking, as on road signs

annotation.surface: A new office block at Waterloo in London is built with a car park included.
annotation.walkthrough: Blackpool Tower is a seaside imitation of the Eiffel Tower in Blackpool, a resort town in north-west England.
annotation.definitionFit: Blackpool Tower is one of England's best-known landmarks.

entries.clue: English course penetrating this writer’s compassionate feelings (7)

indicators.note: to penetrate is to get inside something, so PATH pushes into MY

blocks.note: this writer = the setter, so this writer's = my

annotation.surface: An English lesson that reaches the writer's heart.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'course' a school subject; it is a route. 'This writer' is the setter speaking of themselves.
annotation.definitionFit: A near-synonym: the capacity to share and understand another's feelings, which is what compassion rests on.

entries.clue: Rugby restart has popular centre finally punching oaf (4-3)

indicators.note: a punch drives into its target, so IN and E are driven into LOUT
finally points to the end of the word, its last letter

annotation.surface: A rugby centre punches a thug as play restarts.
annotation.walkthrough: In the surface 'centre' is a rugby position; here it is just a word whose last letter is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: Named by its function: when the ball goes out over the touchline, the forwards line up and play restarts with a throw-in between them.

entries.clue: Place small collection of bets (4)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
the pot is the pool of stakes in a card game

annotation.surface: An instruction to put a few modest bets on.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Place' reads as a verb about betting; it is the noun definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a particular spot and a particular place are the same, as in a nice spot for a picnic.

entries.clue: Snap up hot oatcake wraps (5)

indicators.note: the words 'up hot oatcake' wrap round the answer

annotation.surface: Grab a warm oatcake parcel before it goes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Snap up' looks like one phrase meaning grab; only 'Snap' is the definition, and 'up' starts the hiding place.
annotation.definitionFit: Snap is short for snapshot, an informal picture taken quickly with a camera.

entries.clue: Copy crossing underground cell, according to reports? (10)

indicators.note: what is reported is heard, so the word is given by its sound

blocks.note: trans- is the prefix meaning across, as in transatlantic
a crypt is an underground chamber

annotation.surface: A duplicate smuggled past a prison cell below ground.
annotation.walkthrough: CRIPT is not a word; it only has to sound like CRYPT.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a written record reproduced word for word from speech or another document is a copy of it.

entries.clue: Mum, granny, daughter put together great piece for play (3,3,8)

blocks.note: a man is a piece in chess or draughts

annotation.surface: Three generations of women assemble a fine piece of work for the stage.
annotation.walkthrough: Man and Superman is a play by George Bernard Shaw. The word breaks fall in different places from the pieces: MA NAN D gives MAN AND.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this 1903 comedy by George Bernard Shaw is one particular play.

entries.clue: Crush advanced Ottoman position (5)

blocks.note: a pash is an old schoolgirl word for a crush
A = advanced, as in A level

annotation.surface: A military report of crushing the Turkish line and moving forward.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crush' reads as a verb of battle; it is the noun, an infatuation.
annotation.definitionFit: Pasha was a high rank or title in the Ottoman Empire.

entries.clue: Panhandle city confines American pop (9)

blocks.note: pop is a fizzy drink, such as cola

annotation.surface: A city that bans US pop music.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Confines' looks like a container instruction, but here it is simply PENS in a charade.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Panhandle is the narrow strip of north-west Florida, and this port is its largest city.

entries.clue: They might have eyes, but they won’t be peeled (6,8)

annotation.definition: They might have eyes, but they won’t be peeled

blocks.note: read as people or creatures that can see, and meant as the eyes of a potato, the small buds on its skin
read as eyes not kept peeled, so not alert, and meant literally: these are cooked with the skin left on

annotation.surface: Some watchers have eyes but will not keep them peeled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep your eyes peeled' means stay alert, so the clue sounds like lazy lookouts. The eyes belong to a vegetable, and this one is baked whole in its skin.
annotation.definitionFit: Baked in their skins, these spuds keep their eyes and are never peeled, so the whole clue describes them straight.

entries.clue: Fed up violin maker subject to calumny (10)

indicators.note: in a down clue, up turns FED backwards

blocks.note: used as it stands, then turned up
the Amati family made violins in Cremona
on = subject to, as in on medication

annotation.surface: A violin maker, sick of it all, finds himself slandered.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fed up' reads as one phrase meaning weary; it splits into FED and a reversal instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Calumny is making false damaging statements about someone, which is defamation.

entries.clue: Say G Company fitted with singular shell casing (3,4)

indicators.note: a thing fitted with a part has it installed inside, so COY gets S put into it

blocks.note: Coy is the military abbreviation for company

annotation.surface: Reads like a military order: G Company kitted out with a shell case.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all army: G Company and a shell casing. COY is the army abbreviation for company, and S sits inside it.
annotation.definitionFit: An egg cosy is a cover that keeps a boiled egg's shell warm.

entries.clue: Tiny child violinist failing to start on time (7)

indicators.note: a word that fails to start never gets its first letter out, so FIDDLER loses F
in an across clue, one thing on another sits after it, so IDDLER follows T

annotation.surface: A young violinist who cannot get going on cue.
annotation.walkthrough: A tiddler is British slang for a small child or a very small fish.
annotation.definitionFit: Tiddler is an informal British word for a small child.

entries.clue: Quickly left furniture store with picture (4,1,4)

annotation.surface: Someone rushed out of a furniture shop clutching a painting.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Quickly left' reads as one action; 'Quickly' is the definition and 'left' is just L.
annotation.definitionFit: Like a shot means at once, very quickly.

entries.clue: Criminal back in Parkhurst — old, abandoned (1,3,3)

indicators.note: read the letters backwards
the answer is inside the words that follow

annotation.surface: A convict returning to Parkhurst, an old prison now left derelict.
annotation.walkthrough: Parkhurst is a prison on the Isle of Wight, which suits the crime surface. Read backwards, parkhursT OLD ABAndoned spells A BAD LOT.
annotation.definitionFit: A bad lot is a person of bad character, a criminal type.

entries.clue: Part of picture from the Durbeyfield period? (7)

blocks.note: Tess Durbeyfield is the heroine of Hardy's Tess of the d'Urbervilles

annotation.surface: A fragment of a scene from the age of Hardy's Tess.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Durbeyfield' means the best-known Durbeyfield, Hardy's Tess.
annotation.definitionFit: A tessera is one of the small tiles making up a mosaic picture.

entries.clue: Arrogant, as Bill might be (5-2)

blocks.note: a bill is a poster, which gets pasted on a wall

annotation.surface: Someone called Bill has a reputation for snootiness.
annotation.walkthrough: Bill looks like a man's name; it is a bill poster, which is stuck up.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: an informal synonym for snobbishly proud, and the literal state of a poster fixed high on a wall.

entries.clue: To do with hip cats I managed on island clubs (7)

indicators.note: CATS I are handled into a new order
in a down clue, the anagram goes on top of IC

annotation.surface: Hip cats on a club-filled island, sounding like jazz slang.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hip cats' is jazz slang for cool people, but 'hip' belongs to the definition and 'cats' to the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: Sciatic relates to the hip, as the sciatic nerve runs from it down the leg.

entries.clue: Collection of poems represented real hardship so (1,10,3)

indicators.note: the letters are presented again, in another form

annotation.surface: A book of poems that depicts genuine suffering.
annotation.walkthrough: A Shropshire Lad is A. E. Housman's 1896 cycle of poems; Shropshire is an English county on the Welsh border.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Housman's 63 short lyrics about rural youth and early death form one famous collection.

entries.clue: Journo includes electronic attachment to letter from Prague (5)

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in as a part, so HACK holds E within it

annotation.surface: A reporter sends an email with an attachment to a letter from Prague.
annotation.walkthrough: The email surface misleads: the 'letter' is an alphabet letter and the 'attachment' a mark on it.
annotation.definitionFit: A háček is the small v-shaped accent placed over letters in Czech, the language of Prague.

entries.clue: Film maker sacking satellite boss (4)

indicators.note: sacking someone removes them from the firm, so IO is removed from STUDIO

blocks.note: Io is a moon of Jupiter, removed

annotation.surface: A film company boss fires a satellite TV executive.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boss' is a noun here: a stud is a raised knob or boss.
annotation.definitionFit: A boss is a raised stud or knob, as on a shield.

entries.clue: Harsh, “discontented” Italian Pope? (9)

indicators.note: Italian loses its contents, leaving only the outside letters

blocks.note: Clement is a name taken by many popes

annotation.surface: An unhappy Italian pope proves severe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discontented' reads as unhappy but means emptied of content, and the quotation marks flag the trick. Clement also means mild, so 'in-clement' is its opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: Inclement means harsh, usually of weather.

entries.clue: Exclamation from Spooner upon seeing flying carpet? (2,3)

indicators.note: Rev. Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of two words, so words from him come out swapped

blocks.note: flying = high; its opening H swaps with the M of the next word
a carpet is a mat; its opening M swaps with the H of the word before

annotation.surface: What Spooner cries on spotting a magic carpet overhead.
annotation.walkthrough: My hat! is a dated British exclamation of surprise.
annotation.definitionFit: My hat! is an old-fashioned cry of surprise.

entries.clue: Goddess last seen on gin, regularly pickled (4)

indicators.note: what is last seen of a word is its final letter
at regular intervals, so every other letter
in an across clue, IKE sits on, after, the N

annotation.surface: A divine drinker last spotted on the gin and thoroughly drunk.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' here only places N first.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the winged Greek deity of victory, better known now for the sportswear brand named after her.

entries.clue: Starts to follow at distance, somehow intrigued (10)

indicators.note: take the first letters of follow and at
distance is rearranged in some way

annotation.surface: Tailing someone from afar out of curiosity.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Starts to' covers only two words; distance is not a first letter but the anagram.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having your curiosity strongly caught and held by something.
